description:
I recently moved my own setup from one coding agent to another. It took about 10 minutes and I thought it went well.

The first agent had a lot to carry. Today it has a global instruction file, 114 skill folders (most installed, a few written by me), 189 small memory notes spread across 24 projects and 73 scripts that shell out to its command-line tool. description:
Most enterprises went into cloud computing with the idea that flexibility was part of the deal. Move faster. Scale on demand. Pay for what you use. Avoid long procurement cycles. Stop buying hardware that sits around waiting for peak demand. That was the promise, and much of it was real.

However, many enterprises also made an assumption that turned out to be only partly true: If you need to leave a cloud provider someday, you can. Technically, yes. Practically, not always. description:
Ever since Stephen O’Grady’s The New Kingmakers, we’ve all been trying to figure out how to appeal to developers. Now we’re going to have to figure out how to appeal to their agents. AI agents, after all, increasingly write our code and decide which tools, libraries, etc., to use in writing that code. This means that although developers still own the application, it’s often the agents that own the decisions that factor into building that app.
